Lessons.Title: Represent Measurement Data on Line Plots
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade 3 Unit 6 Lesson5, CCSS 3.MD.B.4, has locally reviewed teacher lesson HTML (SHA256 c1b26874b4d458b3215e77938a5f4f65a39d84d706d370ee64e779e42c1913f6) and preparation HTML (SHA256 d82e8e574efa333db7e09573aa4cd76cc7f6fa0f99925e786e9c8c352b3cef8). Three actual student-facing source sections were reviewed: four multiplication warm-up questions, Go for a Measurement Walk record-your-own length tables, and Let's Make a Line Plot from students' OWN measurements. The standalone original student task PDF and publisher blackline/master art were not located as local files, so this is authoring aligned to local HTML text rather than claimed full publisher PDF/visual parity.

Warm-up Number Talk Multiply Teen Numbers (10 minutes) has four exact ORIGINAL expressions: 3×10=30,3×13=39,6×13=78,3×26=78. Use distributive and doubling relationships: 3×13=3×10+3×3,6×13=2×(3×13),3×26=3×(2×13). Different explained mental strategies are valid; teacher asks for strategy, even though scalar answers are fixed.

Activity1 Go for a Measurement Walk (20 minutes): divide pupils into groups of FOUR. Each group reuses an inch ruler with BOTH halves and quarters marked from previous U06:L03. Take a walk around school, playground, garden, nature area or—if necessary—the classroom, and discuss which objects are safe/suitable to measure, e.g. sticks or leaves. Collect AT LEAST TEN actual object-length measurements per group, measured and recorded in inches in the two-column object/length table (or on lined paper). Do NOT prefill the source's empty table with fictitious predetermined object measurements; original tasks intentionally produce many legitimate unique datasets.

Measurement source mechanics: align zero and endpoints, record nearest whole/half/quarter inch according to the combined ruler, use 1/2 and2/4 equivalence when appropriate. Each entry represents ONE actual measurement of an identified object (repeated lengths are allowed and must each be counted). Teacher checks at least ten entries, correct physical ruler use, recorded units and relevance of selected objects. The teacher preparation notes that the lesson may occupy TWO days if time to gather lengths and build presentations is limited; time extension is optional, not a separate source task.

Activity2 Let's Make a Line Plot (20 minutes): keep the SAME original group of four and its OWN measured list from Activity1. Decide minimum/maximum to cover all measured lengths; select suitable horizontal tick marks of whole inches, halves or quarters so EVERY original observed measurement has one correct location. Put ONE X mark above the right tick for EACH observed object's length, stack repeated measurements vertically, and give the plot a descriptive title and 'length in inches' axis label. Source explicitly offers a blank line as pupil draft, but the final group display is created on a poster. The teacher supplies TWO original line-plot blackline master copies per group which may be cut and JOINED/TAPED/GLUED end-to-end for a longer number line; visual source masters are not copied into this project.

Source Activity2 requires GROUP DISPLAY and a GALLERY WALK (approximately 5 minutes) to visit other posters. Discuss which plots have different numbers of Xs, different minimum/maximum, different object types or different tick spacing, and WHY chosen half/quarter/whole unit increments fit each group's measured sample. Original teacher notes all group plots should have at least10 Xs, not a universal fixed frequency table. Teachers review accurate matching list-to-plot correspondence, scale rationale, presentation and partner mathematical communication.

Original source Section Summary repeats the PRIOR LESSON'S twig quarter-inch line plot from 0 to8, with counts for the 12 marked twig positions starting at4 3/4:1,1,0,1,1,3,5,2,1,3,0,1. This is REVIEW context rather than the dataset groups must reproduce. When 19 original twigs occur in the section summary, do not silently substitute them for students' own group data. Source teacher-gated Cool-down Complete the Line Plot, original full student PDF and original art are not inspected or duplicated. CI tests and Stage D not executed; academic approval, runtime verification, merge and deploy not claimed.

The resulting line plot is NOT publisher-given fixed plot data: it is constructed from students' actual ruler measurements gathered during the measurement walk. Teacher verifies recorded lengths, fractional-unit bins and the resulting class plot.

KeyConcepts.Title: Collect authentic length data
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each selected real object yields one length observation on a ruler calibrated in inches.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a combined half-quarter inch ruler; record each measurement separately.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two different leaves both measuring2 1/2 inches count as two observations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose valid plot scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: The horizontal number line must include every observed measurement as a labeled or inferable tick.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use whole, half or quarter inch increments depending on observed precision and range.
KeyConcepts.Example: If any object measures1 3/4, quarter-inch tick spacing can represent it exactly.

KeyConcepts.Title: Represent a collected dataset
KeyConcepts.Definition: A line plot places one X over the correct numeric tick for each recorded measurement.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Sum of all X marks equals count of measurements in the source list.
KeyConcepts.Example: For ten collected objects, plotted X total is exactly ten.

KeyConcepts.Title: Gallery walk and scale rationale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two groups measuring different objects may legitimately show different intervals and frequency shapes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare quantity, axis span, scale choice, mode and explanation; do not demand matching silhouettes.
KeyConcepts.Example: Twigs may need a larger x-axis range than pine needles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four exact original Number Talk answers
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute3×10,3×13,6×13,3×26 mentally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Start from3×10 then add and double.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source retains each exact expression and its answer.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-party ten-measurement illustration, NOT source data
WorkedExamples.Question: Suppose a group collects ten objects with lengths2,2,2 1/2,2 1/2,3,3,3,3 1/4,3 1/2,4 inches. Make a line plot.
Steps: At2 inches put two X; at2 1/2 two X.
At3 inches put three X; at3 1/4 one X; at3 1/2 one X; at4 one X.
WorkedExamples.Check: Total plotted frequency2+2+3+1+1+1=10. This is explicitly an independent example, NOT a publisher-given fixed plot.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original class gallery walk
WorkedExamples.Question: Why might two valid group plots use different horizontal scales?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare ranges and increments required by actual measured objects.
Steps: One group may find only whole and half measurements.
Another may record quarter measurements needing smaller ticks.
Range/minimum/maximum may differ because of object types.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Different accurate scales can represent different original student datasets
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks chosen scale still covers every observation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Prefill the blank source table with one invented set of ten object lengths as original publisher answers.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source explicitly asks students to measure their own actual surroundings.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Only offer clearly labeled first-party example separate from pupil observations.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use a whole-inch plot when some observations include quarter inches.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Then not all measurements can be located on an exact tick.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Select quarter ticks when dataset needs them.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat two different objects with same length as a single X.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Each object is a separate measured observation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Stack two X marks at the repeated length.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Force all groups to construct an identical 19-twig plot shown in summary.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That data plot reviews earlier original lesson, whereas current activity uses a NEW student-collected dataset.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep review context distinct from the mandatory independent group plot.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count fewer than ten measurements as meeting original group requirement.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Teacher says AT LEAST TEN length measurements per group of four.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks sample size and authentic measurements.

SummaryPoints: Groups of FOUR gather AT LEAST TEN physical inch measurements using half/quarter ruler; student original tables deliberately blank.
Students create their own correctly scaled line plots from actual data, with draft line, title/axis, one X per measurement and a final poster; two blackline copies may be joined.
Gallery walk and comparative reasoning about different scales and plotted shapes are original activities.
Source section summary reuses original19-twig plot as review only, not mandated source student-collected data.
Original publisher student PDF, ruler/line-plot blackline art, gated Cool-down, tests and Stage D unverified.
